author: Rory Mir
title: Google Forcing AI on Students Is BS
content:
Google is rightfully facing blowback for forcing K-12 schools to enable AI if they wanted to keep using Google search. The company quickly backtracked and decoupled and turned off the services by default, but made it clear search will continue to be just another AI chatbot. This mandate forces an ultimatum on educators: accept generative AI or de-google your school.




Students, teachers, and parents across the U.S. are now years into an argument about how schools should respond to the growth of AI-enabled tools. Google decided to skip this debate and take this choice from schools. In August it activated AI chatbot Gemini 

for 150 million K-12 students

 on Google Classroom, leaving educators 

scrambling to respond

. A few months later, Google introduced a new way to turn it off — but now administrators 

would also be turning off Google search

.




Google 

walked this back

 somewhat, clarifying that Gemini, Gemini notebook, and Search will have their own controls and will be off by default. But because of Google’s broader approach to force AI on all search users, this change is still an example of a tech monopolist pushing unwanted changes into the classroom.




Tying AI to Search




It’s no secret that the biggest companies in AI  are 

operating at a huge loss

, in the hope they can follow

 

Uber’s enshittification playbook

. Offer a cheap convenience 

at a major loss

 until old systems atrophy, then flip the script to reduce wages and raise consumer costs—whether that’s paying with cash or with data. 




This puts Google in the odd position of an incumbent, with around 

90% of search traffic

. It needs to not only make good on its own AI investment, but protect its dominance from new AI tools. It’s not just enough to offer its own AI mode, it needs to turn search into AI mode, while engaging in 

clumsy self-preferencing

 that is 

eating its own ad revenue

.




The problem with this approach is the public is split on AI, to put it mildly. Some users will welcome these changes, but the rest are stuck in an all-or-nothing bargain. Anyone concerned  

about the accuracy of AI overviews

 or their 

impact on click-through rates

 for 

online communities

 and 

small publishers

 can just 

deal with it

. The bet is any inconvenience in switching to an alternative is enough to keep you trapped.




Google can and should offer a way to disable AI overviews. Smaller services like DuckDuckGo* and Brave search have simple and persisting AI settings which don’t require login. These services also don't mince words and make a distinction between generated AI summaries, suspected AI results, and the backend use of AI to curate links. 




It’s not enough to point to 

opaque workarounds

, either. Adding “-ai” to your Google search will usually remove AI Overview, but so will “-unicorn”. This trick isn’t meant to be an AI off-switch, it’s a quirk of how AI Overview was implemented and can change at any time. These tricks also don’t generalize well to 

settings for system administrators

. Hacks might work for now, but everyone—including administrators—deserve clear set-and-forget controls for the tools they rely on.




Pushing AI on Schools




De-googling your life isn’t easy, and for schools it can be even more difficult. For decades Google has gone after schools to foster life-long Google users—resulting in many institutions being deeply entrenched in its ecosystem 

despite data privacy concerns

. That’s because schools face major 

switching costs

 when moving to a competitor. It takes more than flipping a setting—it means a lengthy contract process, staff retraining, and a cumbersome migration of past work. 




The difficulty of switching makes granular controls even more essential, particularly for a hot-button issue like generative AI. Few parents would send their kids to 

AI-driven schools

, but they may want their kids to learn tools like search as they exist outside of the classroom. However, many parents and teachers concerned with AI disrupting learning are pushing 

major school districts

 to implement temporary 

AI moratoriums

 for young students. These pauses are meant to make sure any introduction of AI 

fits the needs of students

 

and is done in a way that actually makes sure educators are prepared. 




But in either camp, this is a choice that must be made by schools, not Google. Teachers know more about what their students need than a trillion-dollar tech company, and this expertise should be respected in their own classrooms. 




Google’s self-preferencing and desperate attempt to eventually recoup on an AI money pit must be tempered with more fine-tune controls over generative AI. It’s in Google’s 

own interest

 to stop abusing its dominance to piss off users, advertisers, and school communities. It’s also Google’s 

responsibility

 as an adjudicated monopolist.




*DuckDuckGo is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.

author: Paige Collings
title: Presenting 'Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures'
content:
What does the digital future look like? Who gets to imagine it, shape it, and make it real?




Building a freer, more inclusive digital age requires not only challenging systems of surveillance and control, but also making space for creativity, community, and radical imagination. 




That's why earlier this year with the 

queer arts collective

, we put out a 

call for submissions

 inviting people to explore the intersections of technology, identity, and digital liberation—whether that involved pointing the lens towards an underrepresented issue in digital justice efforts; sharing personal accounts of joy, pleasure, or sorrow under surveillance; or painting wide imaginations for our communities using technology for good instead of carcerality and doom.




And we’re excited to share that the project is now live! 

Desire Lines: Encoding Queer Digital Futures

 explores a digital world that dreams wilder and exists louder. Seven artists share their visions of digital liberation, spanning from early internet-coded yearning to escapist steamy chat rooms and seed-laced battle suits for revolution.

author: David Greene
title: EFF Submission to OHCHR Consultation on Child Rights and Safety in the Digital Environment
content:
“

The safety of young people in the digital environment cannot be assessed without also considering the safety of young people in offline environments. For millions of young people around the world, the digital environment is their safe place, their haven from an unsafe physical environment, community, or family situation. The digital environment may be the best, perhaps only, place for them to find critical safety information and community, to explore ideas that are controversial in their families and larger physical environments, and to otherwise nourish their personal autonomy.




“For these young people, regulatory efforts that limit their access to online services or to certain features they find valuable, make their lives, in total, less safe, even if there has been some marginal safety benefit to their digital environment.




“The OHCHR must thus consider the whole of young persons' lives in any recommendations that come out of this process and not treat ‘safety, physical or mental health, and rights in the digital environment’ as disconnected from safety, physical or mental health, and rights elsewhere.”




So begins 

EFF’s submission

 to the global Call for Inputs on 

Child Rights and Safety in the Digital Environment

 conducted by the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner on Human Rights. The OHCHR is preparing a report on the issue to be presented to the UN Human Rights Council at its 64th session in the first quarter of 2027. The Human Rights Council requested the OHCHR to solicit input from a wide range of stakeholders, including child and youth perspectives, and convene five regional consultations to assess the risks to the safety of the child in the digital environment and best practices to address these risks in different geographical areas, bearing in mind current and emerging business models. 




The OHCHR acknowledges that young people today navigate a digital environment with both “unprecedented opportunities” and “serious and evolving risks,” and sets out a rights-based framing whereby “Children's 'safety' is therefore addressed through the full framework of their rights — with freedom from violence (Art. 19) and protection from exploitation and abuse (Arts. 34–36) as clearly defined obligations, situated alongside privacy (Art. 16), access to information (Arts. 13 and 17), expression (Art. 13), participation (Art. 12), and development (Art. 6). Protection and the full range of children's rights are understood as reinforcing rather than competing imperatives, and measures taken in the name of safety must not be used to restrict the enjoyment of other rights, such as the right to privacy and the right to participate.”




In light of this, EFF’s 

submission

 focused on the current general disregard for young people's speech and privacy rights by regulators around the world, all of whom seem far more interested in empowering parents rather than young people themselves, or meaningfully involving young people in the regulatory process. 

We emphasized the human rights-centered uses young people make of social media that were not specifically set out in the concept note. 

We also explained that too often, policy proposals aiming to remedy the issues of online safety for young people introduce limitations on access to online services and content rather than tackling the specific problems that people experience. 




More specifically, our submission looks at:







the most significant risks to young people’s safety in the digital environment




how digital product design and business models drive risks to children's rights online, including in AI-mediated services




the inclusion of young people’s views in the design, governance, and regulation of digital environments 




how equality and non-discrimination in access and protection can be ensured




the promotion of digital literacy, skills, and empowerment for young people 




the impact of legislative and regulatory measures from the United States to Indonesia and Australia 




importance of broader, more systemic interventions that can address address online harms




how global instruments and processes can protect young people online. 







The internet is where young people learn, find community, explore their identities, access important information, and express themselves. Curtailing these opportunities doesn't make them safer. And requiring everyone to hand over sensitive personal information just to access online spaces creates privacy risks for all users.




As the OHCHR has acknowledged, the solution to the issue of online safety should not require a choice between protecting young people from danger or protecting their rights. Instead of restricting access, governments should focus on the systems that create these risks in the first place; tech companies must be accountable for their design choices, data practices, and surveillance-driven business models; and young people need to be included in the decisions that affect them. 




Read our full submission 

here

.

author: Jillian C. York
title: When the Watchdogs Are Silenced: India's Crackdown on Those Documenting Online Censorship
content:
On November 3, our colleagues at the Software Freedom Law Center, India (SFLC.in) 

received notifications

 from X that the Delhi Police had issued takedown requests targeting 42 URLs. Among the accounts and posts targeted were those belonging to 

SFLC.in

, the 

Internet Freedom Foundation

 (IFF), and X account @geoblockedindia, as well as posts documenting legal notices and instances of online censorship.

 




Takedown requests targeting SFLC.in and other digital rights groups threaten not only their work, but the public’s ability to know when and how online speech is being restricted.

 




The requests cite grounds including hate speech, alleged defamation of the Hindu nationalist organization 

Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh

 (RSS), and concerns relating to safety and security. But the context in which these requests have emerged is particularly troubling: they target organizations and individuals whose work involves documenting restrictions on online expression and making those restrictions visible to the public.

 




In other words, the organizations being targeted are among those trying to tell the public when and how its speech is being censored.

 




SFLC.in is one of India's most important digital rights organizations and promotes innovation and open access to knowledge by helping developers make great free and open-source software, protects privacy and civil liberties for Indians by educating and providing free legal advice, and helps policymakers make informed and just decisions about use of technology. In 2025, we recognized their work with an 

EFF Award

 for Defending Digital Freedoms.

 




IFF

 (the Internet Freedom Foundation) is another of EFF's close allies in India. Like EFF, IFF combines advocacy campaigns and strategic litigation to advance digital rights. They write frequently about internet shutdowns and have filed several lawsuits contesting them.

 




Among SFLC.in's initiatives is its

 

Free Speech Tracker

, which documents instances of online censorship, content restrictions, and account takedowns in India. In a country where government orders to restrict online content are often opaque, this work is absolutely essential.

 

 

Recent legal notices object to the tracker itself, as well as the organization’s documentation of restricted content and geo-blocked material. The allegations against SFLC.in include claims that it is "continuously opposing government directions" and publicly circulating information about restricted content, thereby undermining measures taken in the name of national security and public order.

 




But documenting government censorship is not the same as undermining public safety. Reporting that content has been restricted is not an endorsement of that content, nor does it constitute an attempt to circumvent the law. It is an exercise in transparency and accountability, and one that allows journalists, researchers, civil society organizations, and the public to understand how governments exercise their power over the information landscape.

 




Censorship thrives in the absence of transparency

 




The use of legal complaints and platform takedown mechanisms against organizations documenting censorship creates a particularly troubling dynamic. When those who monitor restrictions on expression are threatened with having their accounts or reporting removed, the result is a chilling effect that extends far beyond the immediate targets. Other organizations or journalists may think twice before documenting controversial takedowns or challenging government orders, and the public loses access to an independent record of decisions that affect its ability to speak and access information online.

 




There is also an important role here for platforms like X. Platforms 

must be transparent

 about the requests they receive, provide meaningful notice to affected users, and ensure that any restrictions are subject to appropriate scrutiny and avenues for appeal. When governments seek to restrict speech, platforms have a responsibility to avoid becoming opaque intermediaries through which censorship is quietly carried out.

 




These developments are part of a broader pattern of pressure on independent civil society organizations working to defend freedom of expression and access to information in India. Digital rights groups play an indispensable role in documenting the effects of government policies, identifying patterns of censorship, and challenging restrictions that undermine fundamental rights. Their ability to do so independently is not a peripheral concern; it is a cornerstone of a healthy democratic society.

 




The right to freedom of expression includes the right to scrutinize the exercise of government power. That includes the right to document censorship, question the reasons given for it, and make that information available to the public. 

 




EFF stands in solidarity with SFLC.in, the Internet Freedom Foundation, @geoblockedindia, and all those working to document and challenge restrictions on online expression in India. We urge the authorities in India to respect the rights of digital rights organizations to conduct their work without intimidation or retaliation, and to ensure that any restrictions on online expression comply with international human rights standards.

author: Rindala Alajaji
title: Reflecting on Digital Rights Wins and Losses in Sacramento
content:
California’s 2026 legislative session has officially adjourned and it’s time to reflect on the wins and losses that have shaped Californians’ digital rights landscape this year. This was the second year of a two-year legislative session, which meant several bills 

resumed their legislative paths from 2025

.




EFF monitored nearly 100 bills in the state over the two-year session. These included proposed regulations on 3D printers, access to social media platforms, police, commercial, and workplace surveillance practices, AI, and other privacy concerns. While we saw some victories, alarming developments also raised serious concerns about the future of privacy protection in the state.




Celebrating Wins




Use of automated decision-making and surveillance in the workplace




Governor Newsom signed vital protections on the use of automated decision-making in the workplace and workplace surveillance tools, specifically 

No Robo Bosses

 (

SB 947

) and 

AB 1883

.




Championed by our 

labor partners

, 

SB 947

 limits how employers can use automated decision-making to fire or discipline workers, including provisions that ensure workers get vital information about automated decisions that affect them, and that an algorithm is not the only authority for these consequential decisions. Alongside it, 

AB 1883

 prohibits the use of workplace surveillance to predict emotions or collect neural data. This stops employers from using potentially biased, invasive, and exploitative forms of AI surveillance at the workplace, marking an important step toward creating workplaces that respect the privacy and autonomy of workers. We look forward to continuing to ensure that technology in California’s workplaces is deployed fairly, thoughtfully, and with respect for all workers.




Protecting against federal overreach




EFF was also grateful to see Governor Newsom sign 

SB 747

, which allows damages lawsuits against federal officials 

who violate the U.S. Constitution

. Victims of constitutional violations deserve a complete remedy and this law also helps deter constitutional violations in the first place. Gaps in current law often make it difficult to seek a damages remedy against federal officials who violate the U.S. Constitution. This bill makes it easier to bring such litigation. Federal law enforcement officials have violated our

 First Amendment right to record on-duty police

 and other newsworthy subjects, and also sometimes violate our Fourth Amendment right to be 

free from unreasonable searches of our phones and laptops

. When this happens, the people who suffer these violations should be able to 

sue these officials for damages

.




Additionally, EFF supported two bills (which are now state law) that clarify and extend California’s shield laws to protect patients, healthcare providers, and others involved in reproductive healthcare and gender-affirming care that is legal in California. After the 

overturn of Roe v. Wade

, California 

enacted

 

numerous shield laws

 to protect people who provide, receive, or help others obtain healthcare that is legal in California. These laws prohibit California agencies and certain companies from helping other states enforce laws that punish this care. Yet the 

federal government

 and coordinated efforts in 

other states

 still 

threaten access

 to these legally protected healthcare services. 

AB 1854

 addresses these threats by expanding coverage to more California businesses and individuals who receive legal demands, creating a notification process so the Attorney General can intervene to stop improper disclosures, and clarifying that law enforcement cannot arrest someone if the Governor refuses an extradition request. These protections serve as a necessary response to real and escalating tactics outside the state targeting lawful reproductive healthcare.




EFF also supported 

AB 1930

 to protect confidential medical records from politically motivated investigations into lawful healthcare, empowering the California Attorney General’s office to meaningfully intervene and respond to out-of-state subpoenas or requests for data regarding protected care.




Young people online




EFF is dedicated to protecting the rights of young people online. We supported a handful of bills on 

digital literacy and cybersecurity education

 that were signed into law, such as 

AB 2071

 on digital wellness instruction and 

AB 2298

 on cybersecurity in educational standards. Unlike 

blanket bans

, these bills address online safety through education rather than prohibition. Young people rely on the internet not just for entertainment, but for 

civic engagement

, 

education

, 

self-expression

, and

 community

—especially vulnerable youth who may 

lack support

 in their physical surroundings.




Real digital safety comes from preparation, not isolation. Research consistently shows that 

open, honest conversations

 about digital literacy and privacy with trusted adults are 

far more effective

 at protecting youth than restrictive censorship laws. Young people themselves recognize this need; in fact, 

AB 2071 was co-authored by a group of students

 actively seeking better resources to navigate their digital lives safely.




EFF and our allies were also able to 

stop the expansion of California’s dangerous age gating law

 from operating systems to browsers. The California legislature 

stepped back from their plan

 to expand the 2025 age-gating law and ultimately removed language from 

AB 1856

 that could have compounded serious threats to users’ speech, privacy, and security just to browse the internet, and positively, removed the burdens on open-source operating systems.




Real digital safety comes from preparation, not isolation




While EFF still believes the underlying law that AB 1856 amends, 

AB 1043, is unconstitutional

, we appreciate that the legislature did not 

expand this problematic age-gating framework

 to browsers. We were also pleased that an earlier amendment to AB 1856 

reduced the threat to the open-source community

 by exempting open-source operating systems. Given these changes, EFF 

removed its opposition

 to AB 1856, and thanks the author for listening to concerns from advocates and developers.




Mourning Losses




Updating California’s Information Practices Act (IPA)




EFF was 

proud to co-sponsor

 

AB 1337

 this session alongside our friends at Oakland Privacy and Assemblymember Chris Ward, who is also the chair of the legislative LGBTQ Caucus. The bill unfortunately failed to cross the finish line after stalling in the Senate.




AB 1337

 would have updated California's foundational 

Information Practices Act of 1977

 and extended its vital privacy safeguards present at the state agency level to counties and cities. Today, city and county governments collect vast amounts of sensitive personal data (from public health records such as vaccinations, to welfare assistance details, to license plate reader data) and administer programs that were likely not contemplated back in 1977. Yet the law has simply not kept up with modern data practices, and California still has no state law governing how local governments handle this information. While we could not build enough political progress to pass the bill this session, closing this local privacy gap remains an urgent need for California.




Social media ban




Another major setback was the passage (and 

subsequent signing

) of a 

social media ban

 for youth under the age of 16 (

AB 1709

).




Technology and the laws that regulate it should support and empower young people, but AB 1709 falls far short of this goal. Using technology is how we learn and build community in today’s world, but laws 

such as AB 1709

 cut young people off from 

essential information and experiences

. They also particularly harm those already facing increased challenges who find safety in supportive online communities that they cannot always access in the physical world.




Technology and the laws that regulate it should support and empower young people




Denying minors access to digital forums or stripping out basic tools needed to navigate them will not make young people safer or healthier in the AI age. Research shows 

social media bans are ineffectual

 while denying young people opportunities to develop their own voices, share their art, practice religion, or engage in politics. These laws also hurt all of us. Age-gating requirements 

force everyone to give up more personal information

. To verify who can pass through online gates, companies will collect even more data, 

concentrating power

 in corporate hands rather than protecting people. AB 1709 is also inconsistent with 

rights to free expression

, meaning California will spend resources 

defending a law that will likely get tied up in court

.




Gutting California’s Invasion of Privacy Act (CIPA) 




CIPA was originally intended to protect personal privacy against surveillance and included a private right of action so consumers could hold corporations accountable in court. This is why EFF and allied organizations spent the two-year session strongly opposing 

SB 690

—a bill we dubbed the "

Corporate Cover-Up Act

" for its attempt to weaken consumer protections in CIPA. Although SB 690 

was narrowed from its original draft

, we asked Governor Newsom to veto it because it strips away the law's private right of action—a vital tool for individuals fighting back against unlawful metadata surveillance. People deserve the right to decide whether to 

bring a lawsuit

, which remains one of the most effective ways to deter corporate abuse. Unfortunately, the Governor signed the bill and even urged the legislature 

to go further next year.

 It's especially alarming to see this disregard for accountability as the federal government and law enforcement agencies seek data from businesses or data brokers to target people based on political beliefs, religious affiliations, or health decisions.




We expect to see further attacks on CIPA next legislative session, as 

Governor Newsom’s signing statement

 called for “additional work in this area” and urged the legislature to “take this on next year to ensure a fair balance between protecting private information and preventing rapacious litigation."




Banning the sale of sensitive personal information




California also missed the opportunity to join other states in restricting the sale of sensitive data. We are deeply disappointed that Governor Newsom vetoed 

AB 1542

, which would have ensured sensitive personal information stays private by banning its sale outright. There's a 

nationwide movement

 to protect consumers by making intimate details off-limits for businesses to sell or share. From 

precise geolocation

 and genetic data to private messages, health records, sexual orientation, and immigration status, sensitive data reveals the most private aspects of our lives. Monetizing this information fuels financial scams, predatory pricing, and warrant-free government surveillance. By 

vetoing this bill

, California not only fails to lead but falls behind other states, by missing a critical opportunity to protect our most vulnerable communities.




3D printing 




The California legislature unfortunately also passed 

AB 2047

, which aimed to make every 3D printer come 

pre-loaded with censorship software

. It's a law that is trying to prevent an act that 

is already illegal in the state

, and 

just won't work

. It was part of a recent sweep of 

misguided state bills

 which purport to go after "ghost guns," but actually 

“enshittify” 3D printers

 by introducing privacy risks and a new way to restrict or upcharge users. Lawmakers even considered including misdemeanor charges that would have impacted people using alternative open-source programs. Fortunately an outpouring of opposition from makers and civil liberties advocates resulted in a bill so limited that, despite having passed and been signed into law, will not affect makers until ASTM International publishes a standard — something the 

organization had not been considering doing

.




Where California Missed the Mark




Consumer privacy




California lawmakers also missed key opportunities to curb commercial surveillance. EFF supported 

AB 2564

, which prohibits retailers from engaging in 

surveillance pricing

, the invasive practice that allows corporations to offer the same product to two different people at two different prices based on scrutiny of their personal data. Unfortunately, the bill stalled on the last day of session.




The legislature also failed to move 

AB 322

, which would have safeguarded the privacy of Californians by placing restrictions on the collection, use, and sale of location data. Last year, EFF 

published a rubric for comprehensive location privacy laws

, outlining baseline standards states should meet to shield individuals from pervasive location surveillance. Since then, states like Connecticut, Maryland, New Jersey, Oregon, and Virginia have 

enacted new consumer privacy restraints on geolocation data

. Yet, even as these states move the ball forward, most of their laws leave significant gaps that still must be filled. California failed to make that change and protect residents from location surveillance.




Automatic license plate readers




California lawmakers have lagged in 

enacting meaningful limits

 on automated license plate readers with all proposed ALPR regulation bills failing to pass since 2022. 

SB 1013

 initially appeared on track to pass with broad support, but ultimately stalled in the final days of the session.




EFF maintains 

high standards for ALPR legislation

, favoring 

full bans or, at minimum

, strict warrant requirements and brief data retention limits. While we remained neutral on earlier versions of SB 1013, EFF and our partners 

ultimately opposed the bill

 after late amendments compromised key privacy protections. The final draft would have doubled the current data retention period and allowed agencies to archive rather than delete data unrelated to active investigations—effectively shifting away from data minimization toward indefinite retention. (We saw 

San Francisco adopt a similar proposal this year

). We encourage California lawmakers to draw from 

our ALPR legislative agenda

 to enact robust safeguards or ban ALPR mass surveillance altogether.




Looking Ahead




Next session, we expect ALPR legislation to be top of mind as 

states across the country

 reckon with the harms the technology has caused. We will also be monitoring the results and action following the 

state’s audit into California’s fusion centers

. Following calls from advocates to address privacy abuses and a lack of transparency, the Joint Legislative Audit Committee 

approved Senator Sabrina Cervantes’ audit request

 in March 2026. This builds on our past experiences working with JLAC audits to expose law enforcement overreach—such as 

the state auditor's damning 2020 report on law enforcement’s use of automated license plate readers

 and our 

2016 push to fix the deeply flawed CalGang database

. The audit will examine the legal authority, governance, and funding of the centers, map out state and private data systems accessed by personnel, and review protocols for handling data breaches and unauthorized surveillance. This audit will mark the first comprehensive review of these facilities in 13 years and should be released by Summer 2027. We hope lawmakers use the findings to rein in these centers and their unauthorized surveillance.




Other “zombie bills” are also expected to return next year, including legislation regarding the use of copyrighted material to train AI systems. Throughout the two-year session, EFF raised serious concerns about 

AB 412

, a bill that would require AI developers to identify and disclose copyrighted works used in generative AI training. We argued that complying with such a mandate is 

practically impossible

, as it demands information that often does not exist and cannot realistically be obtained. While we are glad the legislature paused to consider the best approach rather than rushing this policy forward, we expect legislation targeting fair use and AI training to return next session.




More broadly on AI, 

vulnerabilities

 and 

security issues

 have dominated recent news cycles, and everyday Californians feel real anxiety about the risks of AI. We expect to see numerous bills addressing issues like 

existential risk and kill switches

, as 

Assembly

 and 

Senate

 privacy committees in California have held informational hearings on these topics over the last month.




We hope to work with legislators to address the threats of AI and ensure that technology supports rights, justice, freedom, and innovation for all people. Laws should always ensure that technology empowers rather than oppresses.

author: Hayley Tsukayama
title: Join EFF to Celebrate the Life of Aaron Swartz
content:
Join us to 

celebrate the legacy of Aaron Swartz

 on Nov. 8, 2026. With the organizers of 

Aaron Swartz Day

, we’re honoring his life with an in-person and remote hackathon. This event is supported by several organizations that carry on his work, including the Internet Archive—which is hosting the in-person event—the 

Freedom of the Press Foundation

, 

Creative Commons

 and the 

Free Law Project

.




Aaron Swartz was a 

digital rights champion

 who believed in the need for an open internet. His life was cut short in 2013, after federal prosecutors charged him under the 

Computer Fraud and Abuse Act

 (CFAA) for systematically downloading academic journal articles from the online database JSTOR. Facing the prospect of a long and unjust sentence, Aaron died by suicide at the age of 26.




EFF was proud to call Aaron a friend and ally. We continue to stand with programmers and developers engaged in cutting-edge exploration of technology through our 

Coders' Rights Project

.




Hackathon participants can contribute code, documentation, and design to several open-source and public-interest projects. These include 

Secure Drop

, 

Open Library

, 

Quantifying the Commons

, 

Onion Press

, and our own

.  EFF Director of State Affairs Hayley Tsukayama will also join hackathon participants at the Internet Archive at 11 a.m. for an Atlas of

author: Andrew Crocker
title: We’re Asking the Ninth Circuit to Hold Reverse Location Warrants Categorically Unconstitutional
content:
Yesterday, along with the ACLU, EFF filed an 

amicus brief

 in the Ninth Circuit court of appeals in 

United States v. Spurlock

, a case involving a “tower dump” warrant. These overbroad warrants require cellular providers to turn over location data about every phone in a given area at a given time. This is the first such case to be heard by a federal appeals court since the 

US Supreme Court ruled this summer

 that highly similar “geofence” warrants are searches under the meaning of the Fourth Amendment.




Spurlock 

involves an investigation into two murder victims discovered on the side of a rural California highway. Police also found a car belonging to one of the victims several miles away on the same highway. They quickly sought a tower dump warrant for an area covering this stretch of road, which eventually revealed location data on nearly 1,700 unique phones. Faced with a motion to suppress, the district court relied on a 

Fifth Circuit court of appeals decision

 about geofence warrants to hold that tower dumps are similarly categorically unconstitutional “general warrants” that violate the Fourth Amendment. However, the court refused to suppress evidence on the basis of the “good faith doctrine.”




Our amicus brief on appeal makes several key arguments.




First, we point out that the Supreme Court’s decision in the geofence case 

Chatrie v. United States

author: Katharine Trendacosta
title: Google Summaries Aren't About AI, They're About Lock-In
content:
Whether they call it AI summaries, knowledge panels, or AMP, Google takes actions that are less about functionality and more about locking you into its own ecosystem. Knowing that makes it possible for all of us to choose better services than Google's, defeating their anticompetitive goal. In this case, as it is so often, knowledge is power. 

 




In the old days, when dinosaurs roamed the earth and getting online involved your computer making eldritch shrieking, Google was a website that took whatever you typed in and gave you a list of links that best matched what you were searching for. As it's grown beyond that, however, the core function of Google Search has moved from giving you the best answer to your query to a number of other things, most of them about making money for Google.

 




This is obviously not a new observation. It's at the core of what EFF Special Advisor Cory Doctorow named "

enshittification

." But it's important to remember that whatever shiny new name or technology is wrapped around these tools, it's not about the wrapping, it's about the monetization.

title: Postal Service Surveilled Protest Activities Online With Little Rules, Oversight
content:
The U.S. Postal Service used social media surveillance to monitor and report on protests across the political spectrum, government records show.

The records, disclosed to EFF and other requesters suing the postal service under the Freedom of Information Act, show that the agency’s internet Covert Operations Program, or iCOP, routinely sifted through social media posts organizing and discussing protests with little records of any oversight or legal justification.

EFF filed suit in 2021 after Yahoo News disclosed the program’s existence and how the agency used it to monitor First Amendment protected activities. After years of delays and technical failures that led the agency to lose access to a trove of emails discussing the program, the postal service disclosed records to EFF and several other requesters this year.

The disclosures include a series of bulletins created from iCOP, which show that the postal service used the program in 2020 and 2021 to monitor and circulate information about a wide range of planned protests. They included a planned “Million MAGA March,” a guns rights advocacy event and counter-protest in Virginia, a nationwide Save the Post Office Saturday protest, and planned protests in front of then-Postmaster General Louis DeJoy’s home in Washington, D.C.

Many of the bulletins provide dry descriptions of the events being planned and reference public discussions or events on major social media services. Others seem to imply or anticipate that the protests would turn violent.

For example, in discussing planned national and international protests scheduled for March 20, 2021, the bulletin references potential violence in light of “online inflammatory material.” Yet the bulletin acknowledges that the agency has “no intelligence to suggest specific threats.” This bulletin was described by Yahoo News when it disclosed iCOP’s existence.

Another bulletin discussing an ongoing Black Lives Matter protests in response to police shooting and killing people styles itself as a “National Civil Unrest Update.” The bulletins also recount and monitor threats sent to then-Postmaster DeJoy.

The Postal Service also disclosed three email chains to EFF that, while heavily redacted, show how the agency queried iCOP and disseminated what it found (Read the emails here, here, and here). The government agreed to release the email messages as part of settling EFF’s FOIA suit this fall. To EFF’s knowledge, they are the only existing materials that reflect how the agency queried iCOP.

According to the agency, after Yahoo News disclosed the program in 2021, the postal service renamed it and publicly said that it had stopped issuing bulletins. But the documents do not say that the agency’s social media surveillance stopped.

At the same time, EFF and several other FOIA requesters sought records detailing how the agency used iCOP and what rules the postal service had for using the program and distributing information it gained from surveilling social media. EFF spent years pushing the agency to disclose email communications about the program, which the agency had stored on an external hard drive. Amid these negotiations, someone dropped the hard drive, rendering it inoperable, agency officials said. By the time that happened, the agency had already deleted the underlying email messages pursuant to the agency’s retention schedule.

EFF’s FOIA request sought internal rules, guidance, and training that would show what safeguard the Postal Service imposed to protect First Amendment rights. The agency disclosed very few documents in response to this part of EFF’s request.

For example, a series of slides give an overview of the program, but do not explain how officials used iCOP. The closest thing to internal guideline that the agency disclosed were talking points the Chief Postal Inspector authored in response to questions about iCOP.

The inspector wrote that, “In reviewing social media postings to gather information we did not single out any particular group and did not base what was reviewed on race, religion, gender, sexual orientation, immigration status, or a person’s exercise of First Amendment freedoms.” The statement echoes language in the bulletin stating that its purpose is not to infringe on First Amendment rights; Other parts of the talking points characterize the surveillance as providing officials with situational awareness.

The postal inspector’s talking points go on to say that “the recent attention on iCOP has highlighted opportunities for improvement, including enhanced executive oversight. We have stopped the distribution of the bulletins like the one you have seen in the media reports.”

Setting aside that it’s unclear whether internal oversight occurred or resulted in any changes, the claim that iCOP did not infringe on First Amendment rights rings hollow. As the records disclosed show, surveilling and reporting on social media users’ efforts to organize rallies and protests was a feature of iCOP.

But more fundamentally, the claims by Postal Service officials fail to recognize that surveillance directly chills First Amendment rights. Further, the government can misuse the information it obtained as part of its social media surveillance to harass or retaliate against those exercising their constitutional rights.

Although EFF’s case seeking records about iCOP has ended, we will continue to bring more transparency to the government’s use of social media surveillance and look for ways to challenge the practice, especially when people are caught in the dragnet for exercising the First Amendment rights.

author: Jillian C. York
title: Independent Digital Media Is Not a Privilege Governments Can Revoke: The Fight to Save Egypt’s Mada Masr
content:
On November 11, Lina Attalah, founder and editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet 

Mada Masr

, will face trial for the second time in just two weeks. This time, she faces charges of spreading false news, an accusation that has become one of the Egyptian government's most frequently used tools for prosecuting journalists.

 




The trial follows a conviction on October 27, when Attalah was 

found guilty

 of managing an unlicensed news website. The Mada Masr team had repeatedly applied for a license, but their attempts went unacknowledged. The proceedings took place in a single hearing, which Mada Masr 

states

 included serious violations of her right to a fair trial. She was sentenced to the maximum fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (approximately 55,000 USD), forcibly removed from the courtroom, and held for seven hours until the fine was paid. The court also ordered Mada Masr's closure and the confiscation of all equipment belonging to the organization.

 




The current wave of repression has also targeted 

Matsada2sh

, a fact-checking and open-source intelligence initiative. Its entire six-person newsroom was 

violently arrested

, illegally detained, and interrogated under torture before being charged with terrorism-related offenses and spreading false news. The team remains in pretrial detention.

 




According to CPJ, at least 

25 other journalists

 are currently incarcerated in Egypt.

 




Governments seeking to control the flow of information increasingly rely on a combination of legal harassment, financial pressure, criminal prosecution, and restrictions on the infrastructure that makes independent publishing possible. Egypt's media licensing regime is a particularly troubling example. Requiring news organizations to obtain government authorization to operate creates an obvious mechanism for restricting who gets to publish and whose voices are allowed to reach the public. 

 




The charge of spreading false news is similarly dangerous. Governments around the world have increasingly invoked the language of misinformation to justify restrictions on speech, often without meaningful safeguards against political abuse, as we laid out in our 

recent submission

 to the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights. Governments should never be the arbiters of which reporting is permissible, particularly when that reporting concerns their own conduct.

 




Why Mada Masr matters

 




Founded in 2013, Mada Masr has spent more than a decade doing the kind of journalism that authoritarian governments find most threatening: documenting abuses, amplifying marginalized voices, and reporting on issues that powerful institutions would prefer remain hidden.

 




Its reporting has given torture survivors and the families of political prisoners a platform. It has opened space for debate about reproductive rights. It has brought frontline reporting from Sudan and Gaza, and stood alongside refugees facing xenophobic attacks and security crackdowns.

 




Emerging as a digital-first publication, in a media environment where traditional outlets were increasingly constrained, being purely digital allowed Mada Masr’s founders to build an independent publication outside the structures of legacy media. 

 




At a time when 

only 43% of Egyptians had access to the internet

, going fully digital meant taking a big risk, but it was one that has been rewarding: Despite being blocked by the Egyptian government since 2017, Mada Masr has continued to reach Egyptian and global audiences, and Attalah has received numerous accolades, including the 

Knight International Journalism Award

, the 

Ordre des Arts et des Lettres

, and a spot in 

TIME Magazine’s 100 most influential people

 (2020).

 




Mada Masr has also consistently engaged with technology and advocated for a free and independent internet for the global majority. It has covered dozens of hot-button tech stories in recent years, from 

Egypt’s Cybercrime Bill

 and 

Israel’s use of AI weaponry in Gaza

, to stories about the “

privacy chaos

” caused by biometrics to more 

personal essays

 about the importance of the internet and tech. In August, they launched an 

open call for proposals

 on original critical reporting on artificial intelligence.

 




Mada Masr may be thoroughly Egyptian, but it doesn’t belong just to Egypt. Its team has made into a publication that represents the kind of independent, local, grounded journalism that international audiences need, particularly at a time when international reporting on state repression is lacking. They built on-the-ground networks to center local voices in Sudan (publishing in both 

English

 and 

Arabic

 on the conflict) and Gaza out of a sense of cross-border responsibility and solidarity.

 




This is precisely why its potential closure should concern everyone who cares about a free press. The ability to publish independently, investigate powerful institutions, and to share information without government interference is fundamental to the exercise of free expression. 

 




From solidarity to action

 




The international community has repeatedly expressed concern about restrictions on 

press

 and 

internet

 freedom in Egypt. More than 100 organizations have now joined 

statements

 of 

solidarity

 with Mada Masr, and with 

Matsada2sh

. 

 




These expressions of support matter, particularly when journalists are increasingly isolated and under threat—but solidarity must also translate into sustained political and institutional pressure.

 




The international governments and institutions that maintain relationships with Egypt—including those in the European Union, the United Kingdom, and the United States—should make clear that the prosecution of journalists and the forced closure of independent media outlets are unacceptable. 

 




The cases against Lina Attalah, Mada Masr, and Matsada2sh must be dropped. The journalists who remain in detention must be released. And Egypt's licensing regime, with its profound chilling effects on access to information and independent knowledge production, must be brought to an end.

 




There is a particular urgency to defending independent media at a moment when governments are finding ever more ways to restrict the circulation of information. Whether through internet shutdowns, platform restrictions, surveillance, or the criminalization of reporting, the result is often the same: fewer opportunities for people to understand what is happening around them, to challenge official narratives, and to hold power accountable.

 




We cannot allow the closure of one of Egypt's most important independent newsrooms and the prosecution of its editor-in-chief to become another routine episode in the global erosion of press freedom. Nor should we wait until the last independent journalists have been silenced before recognizing what has been lost.

 




To learn more about Lina Attalah in her own reads, you can read our 

Speaking Freely interview

 from January 2026.

author: Tori Noble
title: Rewriting Copyright Law for Generative AI Would Hurt Everyone
content:
In courts across the country, publishers and creators are suing large AI companies for training generative AI models on copyrighted works. It’s easy to see these cases as a David-and-Goliath showdown between authors and publishers fighting for a cut of Big Tech company profits. But this fight is actually much larger. It affects billions of people who aren’t represented in the case at all, including researchers, artists, activists, journalists, people with disabilities, and anyone who accesses and shares content online.   




That’s why EFF is stepping in to defend the 

public’s

 rights in these cases. Today, EFF filed an 

amicus brief

 in 

In re OpenAI,

 explaining how the court’s ruling on fair use could impact people worldwide. If fair use gets narrowed, it will impede work that benefits the public, like medical research and investigative journalism, and even limit access to privacy protection tools.




Let’s be clear: creators and workers deserve support as AI changes their fields, and Big Tech companies must be held accountable for the harms they cause. But giving copyright holders more control over the web won’t accomplish either of these goals. If the plaintiffs prevail in these cases, courts would have to rewrite copyright law in ways that hurt everyone except powerful media and tech companies.




Rewriting Fair Use Makes Everyone Worse Off




Copyright exists for one reason: to stimulate creativity and innovation in service of the greater public good. Unfortunately, the plaintiffs in this lawsuit are arguing to limit everyone’s fair use rights, in ways that would thwart the basic purpose of copyright. The harms of shrinking fair use will go far beyond generative AI, impacting everyone.




Initial speculation that AI models would be infringement machines, churning out works highly similar to those on which they were trained, 

has proven unfounded

. And courts have already found fair use in cases where copyrighted works were used to train generative AI models, recognizing that training uses those works for 

a fundamentally different purpose

.




Plaintiffs in these cases argue that, even if the use is transformative, using their works to train AI is still unfair, because the AI models could generate new, non-infringing works that might compete with plaintiffs’ own works. They also argue that scraping or downloading the data without permission—or in some cases, from websites containing infringing copies—was independently infringing and/or rendered any subsequent uses of that data unfair.




These arguments would put beneficial research and reporting at risk. First, if copying without permission rules out fair use, the law will never protect transformative uses that benefit us all. Researchers, journalists, and other watchdog groups gather information the same way AI companies do—but they do it to serve the public interest, and often to hold Big Tech itself accountable. For example, journalists and nonprofit researchers have used “crawling” or “scraping” 

to investigate potentially anticompetitive practices by tech companies

, and 

research misinformation and hateful content posted on X

. Their data acquisition techniques are virtually identical to those used by AI giants—but they lack those companies’ deep pockets.




Requiring users to show that copyrighted material was lawfully obtained would also threaten everyday internet use. As EFF’s brief explained, that requirement would “cast legal doubt on the billions of copies we collectively make every day through routine online activities like opening emails, clicking on an embedded link, visiting websites, sharing pictures, streaming music, and watching videos. All of this activity requires intermediate copying.”




Fair use is what lets us all use the internet without being compelled to track the source of every image, video, and article that we click on, and make sure the rights are all cleared.




Additionally, while rightsholders are understandably concerned about competition from AI generated works, 

copyright law exists to 

promote new creation

, not protect authors who published first. Under the plaintiffs’ theory, no one could stand upon the shoulders of giants. Copyright could prevent people from writing new books inspired by themes in a favorite novel or genre, or prevent academic researchers from publishing literature reviews that distill insights from prior research—simply because readers might prefer those new publications over those that came first.




Finally, general-purpose AI models are neither designed nor usually used to create works targeted at any particular market. These models have been used to generate new insights and tools for medicine, science, journalism, art, and accessibility. For instance, an AI-powered tool called 

Be My AI

 uses Open AI’s GPT models to provide visual descriptions for people who are blind or have low vision. Generative tools have also 

accelerated scientific research

, and researchers have used these tools to develop 

new medical treatments and medications

 for conditions previously thought to be incurable.




Mandatory Licensing Would Entrench Big Tech 




Some creators and publishers argue that AI developers should just get a license. But requiring permission for every work used would give the largest companies massive advantages over small competitors and impede academic research. As Professor Lawrence Lessig recently noted:




If all training requires a license, then none but a handful of tech giants will be able to afford the costs of training. That’s not because authors are greedy but because the copyright system is the least efficient property system known to man.







Moreover, creators are unlikely to benefit from these licensing arrangements in many cases. Media and entertainment giants have exploited the imbalance between themselves and underpaid working artists for decades. Trying to help creators by giving them more rights under copyright is, as Cory Doctorow has written, like trying to help a bullied kid by giving them more lunch money for the bully to take. Artists aren’t getting good deals from record labels or publishers now; there’s no reason to think these companies, which already own the copyrights, will treat artists more fairly once they control the data that powers AI.




The Future of AI Is Too Important to Leave to Big Content or Big Tech




AI technologies will affect all of us, and copyright law is ill-equipped to address many of these consequences. The rules governing these technologies should be rules that serve the public—not just the small number of companies that can afford to litigate copyright battles for decades, or settle for billions.

title: Why VPNs Are Worth Defending
content:
Developers of virtual private network (VPN) apps are reporting that their products are again being pulled from Apple’s App Store in Russia. This is an unacceptable crackdown on a vital tool to protect privacy and speech online.

Why? VPNs give people a way to control their own online activities. When you visit a website through a VPN, that website only sees the VPN server's location (well, IP address) rather than your actual location. It's like sending a letter through a P.O. box so the recipient doesn't know where you really live. It can also disguise where you’re accessing information from, which can make it possible to access information banned by your government.

This is an unacceptable crackdown on a vital tool to protect privacy and speech online.

Going after tools that give people the space to communicate and access information freely is a common tactic from the totalitarian playbook. This latest demand comes after several steps the Russian government’s taken to surveil speech specifically on Apple products. In 2024, the Moscow Times reported that Russia’s state media watchdog, Roskomnadzor, went after VPN apps on the Apple App Store, after banning access to Western social media platforms and blacklisting opposition media sites. Russia then blocked Apple’s FaceTime software in 2025, according to Apple Insider.

author: Paige Collings
title: Tech Tips for Parents this Digital Parenting Week
content:
In today’s digital world, the internet is an 

essential resource

 for young people to access information, explore community, and find themselves. But we know that this often comes alongside fears of experiencing online harms like doxxing, grooming, or bullying.




Trying to protect your family from everything all the time is impractical and exhausting, but some thoughtful planning can help families devise a workable plan that meets their needs and addresses their concerns.




That’s why this Digital Parent Week, we’re sharing easy tips on how parents and their children can work together to co-curate a digital safety plan that helps all members of the family enjoy the benefits of technology while protecting their online privacy and safety. 




Start with Open Conversations




Online safety begins with communication, not just restrictions. Talk with a young person about how they use the internet: their favourite apps, games, and social media platforms for example. Creating a supportive environment helps young people feel comfortable asking for help if something goes wrong online.




Together, you can think about:







What do we want to protect? 

e.g., I want to protect a young person’s privacy and mental health when they’re playing Roblox. They love Roblox and use it to communicate and hang out with their best friend, so we’d like to find a way to make it as safe as possible.




Who do we want to protect it from?

 e.g., messages from strangers, staying up too late playing, wasting money on pointless digital junk in games.




How bad are the consequences if we fail? 

e.g, losing some money on a scam or having creepy conversations with strangers that could escalate into something more nefarious or dangerous.




How likely is it that we will need to protect it? 

e.g., I don’t know the likelihood of a stranger messaging you on Roblox because I’m not sure how communication works on the platform, but I’ve heard from their friends that strangers message them all the time in some games.




How much trouble are we willing to go through to try to prevent potential consequences? 

e.g., I’m willing to learn from my child how the game works, play the game with my child, and learn how to work the parental controls. 




Who are our allies?

 e.g., my partner, our parents, as well as a young person’s best friends and their parents.







It's easy to think of a young person's experience on the internet as being totally disconnected and different from your own. But now is a great time to also interrogate your own internet habits, like the sorts of sites you engage with, tools you use, and privacy settings you've set. These questions are as valuable to help you as a parent as they are just an internet user.




Sometimes even just figuring out what conversations are worth having can take some effort, we've put together some ideas to get you started in 

our guide

.




Make Privacy a Family Priority




Digital security training can feel overwhelming but this is why a 

community-oriented approach

 helps. In speaking with your family and friends, you can build out digital security practices that work for you. This makes it more likely that your privacy practices will become second nature to you and your loved ones.




Use secure messaging services for every communication:

 Choosing a secure service ensures that your privacy is protected from government and corporate surveillance. If you can convince your family to get on board, options like Signal provide the most extensive privacy protections out of the box through its use of end-to-end encryption and limited data collection. But we understand that sometimes it's easier to stick with whatever the family already uses for a group chat, like WhatsApp, Apple's iMessage, or Google Messages, so take the time to familiarize yourself with the 

limits of WhatsApp

 and 

RCS encryption

.




Consider the content posted online: 

It's easy to accidentally share personal information through photos, messages, and other content.

 

Children and adults may unknowingly share personal information through photos, messages, location settings and app permissions. Take time together to review privacy settings, check which apps can access the camera or location, and discuss why personal details should be shared carefully. Make sure you have family agreement about when and where to post photos of each other or your home.




Create incident response plans: 

Developing a plan for if or when something bad happens is a good practice for anyone, but especially with younger people. It’s important to strategize with your family around what to do in the event of such things happening, and doing so before an incident occurs is much easier than when you’re presently facing a crisis.




Alongside this, simple steps like using strong and unique passwords on all devices, including those that are shared in the family, can make a real difference. Regardless of age, there’s no time like the present to get started on good security hygiene, and for many that starts with a 

password manager

 and 

two-factor authentication

.




How to Think About Parental Controls




Many sites permit parents to control features such as personalization, algorithmic feed, autoplay, endless scroll, reactions, notifications, and time limits. Talk as a family about which features are important and useful and which are problematic. The conversations above around boundaries and digital literacy are a more effective way to prepare youth for accessing the internet. To develop true autonomy, young people need the privacy to discover the world for themselves without their parents monitoring the contents of every conversation they have.




Explore new apps together and revisit family rules as they grow. These decision points where you’re exploring with a young person what you’re both comfortable with can be good moments to “find your way to a yes” for whatever feature or tool or game they’re asking about. The questions they ask, along with your responses, provide a road map for what to look for in privacy controls that can get you to a place where everyone is comfortable engaging with that technology. 




Small Steps = Big Difference




There is no one size fits all to the tech questions and concerns a parent will face, and keeping young people safe online is not about removing every risk and monitoring every click. This Digital Parenting Week, you can start to focus on what’s important for your family and how to best achieve those goals. 




If you're still not sure where to start, installing EFF’s Privacy Badger on every computer in your household is a great starting point to protecting everyone's privacy.




For more detailed information on all these tips and more, visit 

EFF’s Online Privacy Guide

 for Parents and Youth.

title: Victory! You Can Now Exclude Apps from Siri AI
content:
In the most recent update to Apple’s devices, iOS 27.2, the company has introduced a new setting to “Exclude Apps” from Siri AI, fulfilling one of our asks from 

our Encrypt It Already campaign earlier this year

.




One of our main concerns with new AI features on devices is how those features interact with end-to-end encrypted content, particularly with secure messaging apps. Many AI features require cloud processing, and despite 

privacy protections engineered into these systems

, the content of secure messaging apps may leave a user’s device without their knowledge. That changes the privacy concerns around using those tools. In a perfect world, users would be able to put a barrier up to ensure data from certain apps doesn’t leave the device. Here was our initial ask:




You should be able to tell the operating system’s AI to not access an app, even if that comes at the “cost” of missing out on some features. The setting should be straightforward and easy to understand in ways the Gemini and Apple Intelligence controls currently are not.




At launch, we found the settings to control Siri AI’s app access 

behavior pretty confusing

. You had to toggle several options to block Siri AI off from accessing an app, or disable Siri AI entirely. Turning off Siri AI and 

reverting to Siri Classic

 is, for now, still a good option if you’d prefer to use the older version.
